title: The Beloved Knew His Place and Played Coy
intro: Baha' al-Din Zuhayr wrote this in praise of al-Nasir Yusuf, the Ayyubid ruler of Aleppo and a great-grandson of Saladin; the heading in his diwan dates it to 642 AH (1244 CE). It opens as a love poem: a beloved who plays coy and breaks his promises, a messenger who comes back without his usual smile, and a sleepless lover inventing reasons for the coldness. A pun on the king's title, Salah al-Din, “the soundness of the faith”, turns it to praise of his gifts, his family and their horsemen, then offers the poem to him as a bride who plays coy, as the beloved did in the first line, and closes on thanks. Ibn Hijja al-Hamawi and Ibn Ma'sum quote its turn to praise among their examples of the graceful transition, and Ibn Hijja says of the line after it, “How sweet is what he said after the turn.” Its images borrow from the sciences of hadith and law: reports with an unbroken chain of narrators, a plain text that admits no reinterpretation.

translation: The beloved knew his place in my heart and played coy;
I settled for a promise, and he put it off with excuses.
1.sharh: The beloved knows how much the poet needs him, and so he plays hard to get. The poet would settle for a promise of a meeting, but even that is put off. Arabic love poems often speak of the beloved as “he”, whoever the beloved is.

translation: The messenger came, and I did not find in his face
the gladness I was used to seeing before.
2.sharh: The go-between comes back from the beloved, and the poet reads the answer in his face before a word is said: the cheer he always brought with him is gone.

translation: So I spent the whole day lost in thought,
and lay awake the whole night, tossing.
3.sharh: Day and night go by in worry: by day he turns over what the messenger's face might mean, by night he cannot keep still in bed. The two halves match word for word, day against night.

translation: I began to think that everything which never was
stood plain in my thoughts, a thing imagined.
4.sharh: He imagines every possible reason for the beloved's coldness, even things that never happened, and in his worried mind they look real. The next lines go through them one by one.

translation: Perhaps his phantom came to visit and was turned away
by my waking, and went back in a rage and told tales.
5.sharh: The first guess. In Arabic poetry the beloved's phantom visits the lover in his sleep, but the poet was awake, so it could not reach him; offended, it went back and slandered him. His sleeplessness, born of love, is turned against him.

translation: Or perhaps a breeze, from which I kept our secret all night,
went off and said of me, “He has forgotten.”
6.sharh: The second guess. The breeze carries lovers' news in Arabic poetry; because he hid his secret even from it, it took his silence for forgetting and told the beloved that his love was over.

translation: And I feared that someone else had swayed him,
for it is a branch's nature to sway.
7.sharh: The third guess, and the one he fears most: a rival. The beloved is slender as a branch, and a branch bends to every wind, so his fickleness is only his nature.

translation: I think he wanted something new; how often
a shirt grows old on a man, and he changes it.
8.sharh: The fourth guess: the beloved has simply tired of him and wants someone new. The poet bitterly likens himself to an old shirt, worn until it is thrown away for another.

translation: He always wants me far, while I seek him near;
were I his neighbour, he would move house.
9.sharh: Now he stops guessing and states the plain fact: the beloved keeps away as hard as he pursues him. Were they neighbours, the beloved would rather move than live near him.

translation: I fell for him: like a branch, dark and slender,
and loved him: like a gazelle, black-eyed, his lids dark as kohl.
10.sharh: For all that, he loves him. The two halves run in parallel, each with a comparison and two marks of beauty: a branch for the beloved's figure, a gazelle for his eyes.

translation: He shamed the sun and the gazelle: one is now
in mid-sky, the other in the midst of the desert.
11.sharh: His beauty outshone the sun and the gazelle, and both fled in shame, one to the middle of the sky, the other deep into the desert. An old name for the sun, ghazala, is also the word for a doe, so the line pairs it with the gazelle, ghazal.

translation: What a wonder, a heart never free of the ache of love,
forever longing for a time long gone.
12.sharh: He marvels at his own heart: never free of love's pain, yet always homesick for the past, as if it had once been happier. The same word, khala, ends both halves, first meaning “free of” and then “gone by”.

translation: And at the traces of a body that passion almost burned:
had the tears not come in time, it would have caught fire.
13.sharh: He also marvels at his body, wasted by love until only traces are left, like a ruined camp. Love's fire nearly set it alight; only his tears, falling in time, put it out.

translation: And at a love whose story I kept by heart and hid,
and found my tears had passed it on in an unbroken chain.
14.sharh: He memorised his love's story and told no one, but his tears told it for him, one after another. The words come from the science of hadith, where reports are memorised and handed down through chains of narrators; the verb for “handed down” also means “watered”.

translation: In love I would gladly humble myself, but
Salah al-Din will not let me be humbled.
15.sharh: A lover is expected to abase himself before the beloved, and he would, but his patron has raised him too high for that. Salah al-Din is the king's title and also means “the soundness of the faith”, which forbids self-abasement. With this line the poem turns from love to praise.

translation: I paved the way for his praise with tender love verses,
wanting to pray the voluntary prayer before the obligatory one.
16.sharh: The love verses were only the prelude. Praising the king is his duty, like an obligatory prayer, and the love poem before it is like the extra prayers a Muslim may offer first. Ibn Hijja quotes the line and says, “How sweet is what he said after the turn.”

translation: A king by whose nearness I tower over kings;
from him I wear the robe of honour, trailing long.
17.sharh: Being close to this king lifts the poet above all other kings, so he needs none of them. Honour is a robe the king has dressed him in, long enough to trail behind him, a sign of plenty.

translation: I raised my voice and called, “Yusuf”,
and a king answered me, giving long and lavishly.
18.sharh: He has only to call the king by his name, Yusuf, and the answer comes at once, not in words but in gifts, generous and lasting. Calling on him is like a prayer that is granted as soon as it is said.

translation: Then I turned and found favours all around me;
how swiftly they came to me, how soon.
19.sharh: In the moment it takes to turn his head, he is surrounded by the king's gifts. The wonder is not only their number but their speed: they came before he could ask.

translation: I pulled down the branches of my wishes, already bending,
and milked the udders of his gifts, already full.
20.sharh: Everything he wants comes easily: his wishes are branches so laden they bend to his hand, and the king's gifts are a she-camel whose udders are full before he milks. Both images are of plenty that asks no effort.

translation: He subdued Time, whose blows had struck me,
until Time walked on foot in my service.
21.sharh: Time, the old enemy of Arabic poets, had been battering him. The king tamed it so thoroughly that it now walks beside the poet like a servant beside his master's horse.

translation: Whenever I look, I find that even some of his gifts
hold glories, noble deeds and high rank.
22.sharh: His gifts are not just wealth: even a few of them bring honour, things to be proud of and spoken of. Whoever receives them gains standing as well as riches.

translation: The report of generosity comes down from him with its chain whole;
why then do the clouds pass it on with a broken one?
23.sharh: He is the true source of generosity, and its story comes from him on the best authority. Beside him the clouds, the usual image of giving, are a weak, second-hand source. Musnad and mursal are terms from the science of hadith; mursal also suggests rain sent down.

translation: He is of a house that surpassed all kings in lordship,
in fortune, in bounty and in grace.
24.sharh: Praise of the king becomes praise of his family, the Ayyubids, the house of Saladin. They outdo other kings in four things, set out in a row: rank, good fortune, giving and kindness.

translation: As if, on the day they ride out, the back of the earth
were dressed by them in a fine, loose-woven cloak.
25.sharh: Their horsemen are so many that when they ride out they cover the face of the earth as a cloak covers a body. The cloak is light and open, as spread-out ranks of riders would be. Or the cloak may be the fine dust their horses raise over the ground.

translation: Each of them bull-necked in battle, as if
he had put on a pool and brandished a stream from it.
26.sharh: A riddle-like image: the warrior's coat of mail, its rings like ripples, is a pool of water, and his gleaming sword is a stream running out of it. The second half is word for word in a line by an earlier Andalusian poet, al-A'sha the grammarian.

translation: Ask, and you ask a pouring rain;
meet them, and you meet a lion guarding its cubs.
27.sharh: Ask any of them for a gift and it pours on you like steady rain; meet one in battle and he is a lion with cubs to defend, a lion at its most dangerous. The halves echo each other in sound: ghaythan musbalan, laythan mushbila.

translation: My lord, I bring her to you, a maiden in her bloom,
a virgin who offers her excuses and pleads her innocence.
28.sharh: The poem itself is the bride: young, untouched, never heard before. She comes apologising because she is late (the next line says why). The word for her excuse, udhra, plays on adhra', “virgin”.

translation: She carried praise as heavy as hills, and so was slow;
forgive a slow one who comes to you heavy-laden.
29.sharh: He turns the poem's lateness into a compliment: it took long because it carries so much praise. This is the excuse the line before announced.

translation: She knew how dear she was to you, and how lovely,
so she came to show you her airs and her swaying walk.
30.sharh: The end of the poem answers its beginning. The beloved of the first line knew his place and played coy; now the poem knows its place with the king and comes to him with the same airs.

translation: A Bedouin, if you like, or a town girl:
her fragrance joins lavender and aloeswood.
31.sharh: The poem has the strength of the desert and the polish of the town. The two scents follow the order of the first half: lavender grows wild in the desert, while aloeswood is burned in city homes.

translation: Had she been of those whose age came earlier,
she would have stopped Ziyad and Jarwal from speaking.
32.sharh: Had this poem existed in the classical age, the great poets of that time would not have dared to compete with it. He names two of them by their given names rather than their famous nicknames, al-Nabigha and al-Hutay'a.

translation: Love and praise: I spent the night lost in them both,
like wine mixed with clear, sweet-flowing water.
33.sharh: The two parts of the poem, love and praise, are blended into one, as wine is mixed with water before it is drunk. Neither can be tasted apart from the other.

translation: So they joined into a necklace of delightful stringing,
and a necklace is best with gems between the beads.
34.sharh: Love and praise alternate in the poem like beads and gems on one string. Arabic uses the same word, nazm, for stringing beads and for composing verse.

translation: O you, in whose praise every word I say is true,
as if I were reciting a book sent down from heaven.
35.sharh: He insists that his praise is no flattery: every word of it is as true as scripture. It is a hyperbole that claims to have none.

translation: O you, to whom my loyalty is a plain text,
and a plain text, the scholars hold, is never explained away.
36.sharh: His loyalty is as clear as the plainest text of the law. Jurists hold that such a text, a nass, is taken at its word; his loyalty, likewise, admits no other reading.

translation: My life with you has been sweet; I want
no other, and if I ever do, may it not be sweet.
37.sharh: Life at the king's side is so sweet he wants no other. The line ends with a curse on himself should he ever change his mind, using the word for “sweet” that began it.

translation: I have thanked your generosity with all thanks, knowing
I cannot repay even part of it, no, and no.
38.sharh: The poem closes on gratitude: however much he thanks the king, it falls short of even part of what he owes. The repeated “no” says he cannot repay even a fraction of a fraction.

5.1.2.head: طَيف
5.1.2.meaning: Tayf: the image of the beloved that visits a sleeper in dreams.

10.2.3.head: أَحوَر
10.2.3.meaning: Ahwar: with eyes whose white is very white and whose black is very black.

10.2.4.head: أَكحَل
10.2.4.meaning: Akhal: with lids naturally dark, as if lined with kohl.

11.1.2.head: الغَزالَة
11.1.2.meaning: Ghazala: the sun, above all at sunrise.

13.1.1.head: رُسوم
13.1.1.meaning: Rusum: the traces of an abandoned campsite; here, what love has left of his body.

14.2.5.head: مُسَلسَل
14.2.5.meaning: Musalsal: in hadith study, a report whose narrators all hand it on in the same way, link after link.

15.2.2-3.meaning: Salah al-Din: the title of al-Nasir Yusuf, Ayyubid king of Aleppo and later of Damascus, great-grandson of the famous Saladin; Hulagu had him killed in 659 AH (1261 CE).

18.1.5.meaning: Yusuf: the king's own name, Joseph.

22.2.3.head: المَآثِر
22.2.3.meaning: Ma'athir: noble deeds that people tell of.

23.1.5.head: مُسنَد
23.1.5.meaning: Musnad: in hadith study, a report with an unbroken chain of narrators back to its source.

23.2.4.head: مُرسَل
23.2.4.meaning: Mursal: a report with a link missing from its chain, and so weaker.

26.1.3.head: أَغلَب
26.1.3.meaning: Aghlab: thick-necked, like a lion; a mighty man.

26.2.2.head: الغَدير
26.2.2.meaning: Ghadir: a pool left behind by a flood.

28.1.5.head: كاعِب
28.1.5.meaning: Ka'ib: a girl in her first youth.

30.2.4.head: تَعَسُّل
30.2.4.meaning: Ta'assul: a quick, swaying gait, like a trotting wolf's.

31.2.2.meaning: Khuzama: lavender, a sweet-smelling desert plant.

31.2.4.head: المَندَل
31.2.4.meaning: Mandal: Indian aloeswood, burned as incense.

32.2.2.head: زِياد
32.2.2.meaning: Ziyad: Ziyad ibn Mu'awiya, better known as al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani, a great pre-Islamic poet.

32.2.5.head: جَروَل
32.2.5.meaning: Jarwal: Jarwal ibn Aws, known as al-Hutay'a, a poet who lived into Islam, famous for satire.

34.2.5.head: مُفَصَّل
34.2.5.meaning: Mufassal: a necklace with a gem set between every two beads.

36.1.5.head: نَصّ
36.1.5.meaning: Nass: in Islamic law, a text so clear it allows only one meaning.
